🚀 We are a team of AI, Data, Backend, and Flutter enthusiasts excited to turn NASA challenges into real solutions.
We combine diverse skills to build complete prototypes, learn, experiment, and collaborate while pushing beyond what we already know. 🌌🤖
summary:
As more private crews, tourists and researchers travel to low Earth orbit, every commercial mission needs a way to keep people healthy without a hospital next door. Astronaut Health Monitoring is a scalable software service that turns crew measurements (heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, sleep and radiation dose) into a clear status and next steps. A local AI assistant explains each alert using NASA research.
It is designed to be offered to commercial station operators and mission providers as a per-mission subscription. It runs on board without a constant cloud link, so it supports safer missions while keeping the cost of medical support under control
details:
1. Project Overview

OrbitCare is an AI-assisted astronaut health monitoring application designed to support crew well-being during space missions.

It provides a centralized platform for recording, monitoring, visualizing, and analyzing health-related data, helping astronauts and mission support teams better understand health trends and identify measurements that may require attention.

The project combines mobile technology, backend infrastructure, data analysis, and AI-powered assistance into an integrated health-monitoring prototype.

2. The Problem

Space missions introduce unique challenges to human health monitoring. Astronauts operate in demanding environments where continuous awareness of their physiological condition is important, while communication with Earth may be limited or delayed.

Managing multiple health indicators and understanding changes over time can also be challenging.

OrbitCare addresses these challenges by organizing health information into an accessible platform that supports monitoring, analysis, and informed decision-making.

3. Core Features

  • Secure Authentication: User registration, email verification, login, password recovery, and secure session management.
  • Health Dashboard: A centralized overview of important health indicators and monitoring statistics.
  • Vitals Tracking: Recording and managing physiological measurements, including heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, respiratory rate, and body temperature.
  • Health Visualization: Historical measurements and graphical representations of health trends.
  • Health Alerts: Notifications for health-related conditions, with alert management and acknowledgement.
  • Periodic Reports: Aggregated daily, weekly, and monthly health summaries.
  • AI Health Assistant: AI-assisted explanations and contextual health insights based on structured medical knowledge.
  • Cognitive State Monitoring: An experimental research module exploring crew attention-state monitoring.

4. AI and Data Intelligence

The AI component combines two main approaches:

Rule-Based Health Assessment

A deterministic rule engine evaluates available health measurements against configurable thresholds to determine their corresponding status.

AI-Powered Knowledge Assistant

A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture uses a curated knowledge base to provide contextual explanations and relevant information.

The system separates health-status decisions from AI-generated explanations, helping maintain transparency and reduce unsupported AI recommendations.

Experimental Cognitive State Monitoring (DEC-001)

An additional research module explores the analysis of physiological signals to investigate four cognitive states:

  • Baseline
  • Channelized Attention (CA)
  • Diverted Attention (DA)
  • Startle / Surprise (SS)

This research uses NASA's Flight Crew Physiological Data for Crew State Monitoring (SHARP-1) dataset as its intended research source.

The module includes signal preprocessing, feature extraction, signal-quality assessment, and experimental machine-learning evaluation pipelines.

Importantly, this module is still experimental. No trained or validated operational cognitive-state model is currently included in the repository.

5. System Architecture and Technologies

OrbitCare follows a modular architecture consisting of three primary components.

Mobile Application

  • Flutter
  • Dart
  • Secure local session storage

Responsible for the user interface, health dashboards, measurements, reports, alerts, and interaction with backend services.

Backend Infrastructure

  • Node.js
  • Express.js
  • MongoDB
  • Mongoose
  • JWT Authentication

Responsible for authentication, data storage, API management, validation, and communication between the mobile application and AI services.

AI and Data Science

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Scikit-learn
  • SciPy
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
  • Signal Processing

Responsible for health-data analysis, rule-based assessments, knowledge retrieval, and experimental cognitive-state research.

The components communicate through REST APIs using structured JSON data.

6. Data Management and Reliability

The platform emphasizes structured data handling and transparency.

Key considerations include:

  • Distinguishing real, simulated, and synthetic data.
  • Preserving data-source information and provenance.
  • Validating incoming measurements.
  • Handling missing or invalid health information.
  • Providing structured API responses.
  • Maintaining clear limitations around experimental AI outputs.

7. Safety and Limitations

OrbitCare is an educational and research prototype, not a clinical diagnostic system or flight-certified medical product.

It does not replace medical professionals or operational decision-making.

Health thresholds require appropriate medical review, and experimental AI components must not be interpreted as medically validated predictions.

The cognitive-state monitoring module currently provides research infrastructure and evaluation capabilities, rather than a validated operational monitoring solution.

8. Future Development

Potential future improvements include:

  • Expanding the medical knowledge base.
  • Improving health-data analysis and personalization.
  • Developing individual health baselines.
  • Evaluating experimental ML models using appropriate research protocols.
  • Exploring wearable-device integration.
  • Exploring integration with spacecraft health telemetry systems.
  • Improving offline availability and system reliability.

These capabilities remain development goals and require appropriate technical and medical validation before operational use.
